lead: The PIC18F452 (Microchip) and MSP430 (Texas Instruments) are alternatives to the 8051. Both read a sensor, run a control loop and drive a pin, with different trade-offs. The PIC has an 8-bit data path and 16-bit instruction words in flash; its 8-bit data address forces 1536 bytes of RAM into banks selected by the BSR. The MSP430 has a 16-bit RISC core, 16 registers and named sleep modes.
prereq: You need Chapter 4.1 for the 8051 register and memory map, Chapter 4.6 for Embedded C, and Unit 1 for Harvard versus von Neumann and RISC versus CISC.

blocks.text: The PIC18F452 is Harvard-architecture: program and data memory use separate buses, so the CPU fetches the next instruction while reading or writing data. Flash is 32 KB = 32,768 bytes. Instructions are 16-bit words (a few use two words), so flash holds 32,768 ÷ 2 = 16,384 words. The data path is 8 bits: WREG holds one byte.

Data memory has 1536 bytes RAM plus 256 bytes EEPROM. An 8-bit address reaches 256 locations, so RAM is divided into banks of 256 bytes: 1536 ÷ 256 = 6 banks. The low four bits of the Bank Select Register (BSR) select the bank; only banks 0–5 exist. The access bank is a fixed window over part of bank 0 and bank 15 (special function registers), so it ignores BSR.

Key registers: WREG (accumulator), STATUS (carry, digit carry, zero, overflow, negative flags), BSR, and TRISA–TRISE (port direction). A 1 in a TRIS bit makes that pin an input; 0 makes it output. Code is C with XC8 or assembly in MPLAB X, loaded by in-circuit serial programming.

blocks.where: Tcy is the instruction cycle time in seconds, Fosc the oscillator frequency in hertz, and 4 is the number of oscillator periods one instruction takes.

blocks.text: Bank switching is the cost of the small address field. The C compiler loads BSR before touching a banked variable and keeps hot variables in the access bank. Hand-written assembly must do the same; each switch costs an instruction.

Table reads fetch constants from flash. A seven-segment table lives in flash because flash is large and RAM small. TBLRD copies one byte from byte address TBLPTR into TABLAT; then a move brings it to WREG. Entry n starts at byte 2n, so add 2 for the next entry. The 8051 does this with MOVC A,@A+DPTR (Unit 3).

The MSP430 is a 16-bit RISC microcontroller for battery-powered instruments. It has 16 registers R0–R15, each 16 bits. R0 is the program counter, R1 the stack pointer, R2 the status register (carry, zero, negative, overflow flags and interrupt-enable bits), and R3 a constant generator producing 0, 1, 2, 4, 8 or −1 without an operand field. R4–R15 are general purpose. Register-to-register instructions are one 16-bit word.
Peripherals are memory-mapped: timer, port, UART, SPI and I2C registers share the 16-bit address space with RAM, so ordinary moves and C pointers work on hardware registers.

The clock module saves power. A digitally controlled oscillator (DCO) starts in microseconds and can be switched off, so it costs little energy while the CPU sleeps. A 32.768 kHz watch crystal drives ACLK for the timer. Software selects the CPU clock MCLK and subsystem clock SMCLK. Low-power modes LPM0–LPM4 switch off parts of the clock tree: LPM0 stops only the CPU clock; LPM3 keeps ACLK and timer alive with DCO off; LPM4 stops everything. Any enabled interrupt returns to active mode. Tools: Code Composer Studio with Embedded C, or GCC.

sections.h3: The three families side by side

blocks.text: The differences are design choices. The 8051 and PIC18F452 are 8-bit; the MSP430 is 16-bit, so a 16-bit add handles two data bytes in one instruction and a pointer fits in one register. Banking is PIC-only: the 8051 has at most 256 bytes RAM, so a direct address always fits. The MSP430 has no separate SFR space. The MSP430 grades low power into LPM0–LPM4; the 8051 has Idle and Power-down; the PIC18 has Sleep. The MSP430 returns from LPM0 within a clock cycle and from LPM3 in microseconds because the DCO restarts.

figure.caption: The three families side by side. The PIC keeps 8-bit data in six banks of 256 bytes reached through the BSR, and the MSP430 trades width for a 16-bit core with sleep modes.

spec.aria: Tree comparing the 8051 with PIC18F452 and MSP430, showing that the PIC uses banked RAM of six banks of 256 bytes and the MSP430 uses low-power modes up to LPM4.

examples.question: A PIC18F452 has 32 KB flash, 1536 B RAM, 16-bit instruction words, and 4 oscillator periods per instruction. The crystal is 10 MHz. Find (a) instruction words in flash, (b) 256-byte RAM banks, (c) instruction time.
examples.answer: The flash holds 16,384 instruction words, the RAM is split into 6 banks, and one instruction takes 0.4 µs (400 ns).
examples.check:
flash = 32 * 1024
words = flash // 2
banks = 1536 // 256
fosc = 10_000_000
tcy = 4 / fosc
print(words)
print(banks)
print(round(tcy * 1e6, 6))

examples.question: An MSP430 draws 300 µA active at MCLK = 1 MHz and 1 µA in LPM3. A 32.768 kHz crystal wakes it for 100 µs every 10 ms. Find average current.
examples.answer: The average current is about 3.99 µA, roughly 75 times less than running continuously at 300 µA.
examples.check:
active = 300e-6
sleep = 1e-6
duty = 100e-6 / 10e-3
avg = duty * active + (1 - duty) * sleep
print(round(duty, 6))
print(round(avg * 1e6, 6))

traps: PIC flash is counted in 16-bit words, not bytes: 32 KB = 16,384 words.
One PIC instruction takes 4 oscillator periods, so rate = Fosc ÷ 4. At 10 MHz, Tcy = 0.4 µs, not 0.1 µs.
In a PIC, TRIS = 1 makes an input. This differs from the 8051 rule of writing 1 before reading a pin.
MSP430 R0–R3 are not general purpose: PC, SP, status, constant generator.
MSP430 LPMs differ: LPM0 stops CPU clock; LPM4 stops all clocks and exits only by interrupt or reset.

quiz.q: Name the register that selects the active RAM bank in the PIC18F452 and state how many banks the part implements.
quiz.a: The Bank Select Register (BSR). Its low four bits hold the bank number; the part implements banks 0–5, that is six banks.

quiz.q: Why does the PIC18F452 need bank switching when the 8051 does not?
quiz.a: A PIC instruction carries only an 8-bit data address, reaching 256 locations, but the part has 1536 bytes RAM, so the BSR supplies a bank number. The 8051 has at most 256 bytes RAM, so one direct address covers it.

quiz.q: A PIC18F452 runs from a 20 MHz crystal. Find the instruction cycle time Tcy.
An MSP430 instruction word is 16 bits and the CPU has 16 registers. How many bits are left for opcode and other fields if a register is named by its number?
quiz.a: 16 registers need log₂ 16 = 4 bits. A register-to-register instruction names two, using 8 bits, leaving 8 bits. In the real encoding, 4 are opcode and 4 hold addressing-mode and byte/word bits.

quiz.q: Why does the MSP430 map peripherals into the same address space as RAM instead of giving them a separate SFR space?
quiz.a: One address space means ordinary moves, bit and arithmetic instructions work on peripheral registers; no special I/O instructions are needed; C pointers can address hardware directly; and the compiler uses the same code for a variable and a timer register.

quiz.q: A coin-cell product must run for a year. Compare an MSP430 sleeping in LPM3 and waking for 100 µs every 10 ms at 300 µA with the same chip running continuously at 300 µA.
quiz.a: The waking version is active for 100 µs ÷ 10,000 µs = 0.01 and sleeps at about 1 µA, giving 0.01 × 300 + 0.99 × 1 = 3.99 µA average. Continuous draws 300 µA, about 75 times more, so the sleeping design lasts about 75 times longer on the same cell.

quiz.q: What does the PIC18F452 table read sequence do, and why is the table kept in flash?
quiz.a: TBLRD copies a byte from the byte address in TBLPTR into TABLAT; a move then takes it to WREG. Flash holds the table because it is larger than RAM and the constants never change; add 2 to TBLPTR for the next entry.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern parts keep the same programming model and add hardware the older syllabi do not cover: Microchip's PIC18-Q10 family puts configurable logic and an ADC with computation beside the CPU, and the MSP430FR series replaces flash with ferroelectric RAM, so writes cost less energy and survive power loss. Ultra-low-power design now competes with ARM Cortex-M0+ parts, which is why energy per operation, not clock speed, leads datasheets.
